title: Avoid These 7 Common Crypto Scams and Mistakes
description: Avoid costly crypto mistakes. Learn how to spot common cryptocurrency scams and beginner errors before they wipe out your entire investment.
alt: Person looking concerned while checking crypto wallet on a phone

content.text: Crypto attracts two kinds of trouble: scammers who target newcomers, and honest mistakes that can't be undone because there's no bank to call. Experience doesn't make you immune to either. Here are seven of the most common, and what to do about each.

Scams work on smart people too, because they target emotion, not intelligence. They create excitement (you're about to get rich), fear (your account is about to be locked) or trust (someone friendly is helping you), and then ask you to act before you've had time to think. Knowing the patterns below won't make you immune, but it will give you the pause that most victims never get.
1. Phishing Scams

A message arrives, apparently from an exchange like Binance or Coinbase, saying your account has a problem and you need to log in. The link goes to a near-perfect copy of the real site, and the moment you type your password it belongs to someone else. Never log in through a link in an email or direct message. Bookmark the exchange's real address and use that. Where it's offered, switch on the anti-phishing code on Binance, Crypto.com, Bybit and other major platforms: a code you choose appears in genuine emails from the exchange, so one without it is an instant red flag.
2. Fake Giveaways

The pattern never changes. An account impersonating a celebrity or well-known crypto figure promises to double whatever you send, or pushes you towards a new platform or memecoin. Anything you send is gone for good, and no real giveaway asks you to pay first. If it sounds too good to be true, it is. Hype on social media isn't evidence that a project is legitimate, however many accounts are repeating it.
3. Pump and Dump Groups

Telegram and WhatsApp groups promise a coin that's about to explode. What's actually happening is that the organisers buy cheaply, hype the coin until newcomers pile in, then sell at the top. The people who joined late are the ones the early buyers sell to, and they're left holding a token nobody wants. If your reason for buying is that a group chat told you to hurry, that's your cue to stop.
4. Fake Wallets and Exchanges

Scammers build apps and websites that look identical to real wallets and exchanges. Some advertise fake arbitrage deals or slightly inflated prices to get you to deposit; once you do, the money doesn't come back. Download wallets only from the provider's official site, check the developer's name in the app store, and read reviews before you trust any platform with funds.
5. Sending Funds to the Wrong Address

Bank transfers can often be reversed. Crypto transfers can't. Paste the address rather than typing it, check the first and last few characters, and use a QR code where you can. Make sure the network matches too: sending a token like USDT over the wrong network is a classic way to lose money, even with a perfectly correct address. For larger amounts, send a small test transaction first and confirm it arrives.
6. Investing Without Research (FOMO)

Fear of missing out pushes beginners towards tokens simply because they're trending. Before putting in any money, find out what the project does, who's behind it, how many tokens exist and who holds them, and whether anyone would use it if the price stopped mattering. A simple test: if you can't explain what the project does in one sentence, don't invest.
7. Sharing Your Private Keys or Seed Phrase

This is the most expensive mistake in crypto. Your seed phrase is the master key to your wallet, and whoever has it controls everything inside. Don't give it to friends, to customer support, or to anyone offering to help you recover an account. No legitimate platform will ever ask for it. Write it on paper, store it offline, and never type it into a website or photograph it.
Be especially wary if you've already been scammed. "Recovery" services that contact you out of the blue are usually a second scam aimed at the same victim.
Other scams worth knowing about

Investment romance scams start with a friendly stranger on a dating app or social media who builds trust over weeks, then mentions how well they're doing with crypto and invites you to try "their" platform. The platform shows fake profits to encourage bigger deposits, then blocks withdrawals or demands "taxes" and "fees" before releasing your money. These are often called pig-butchering scams. Someone you've never met in person shouldn't be guiding your investments.

Fake support works like this: you post about a problem on social media and "support agents" appear in your replies or messages with a helpful link. Real exchanges don't contact you first. Go to the official app or site and use the support channel there.

Rug pulls and honeypot tokens are common with brand-new memecoins. In a rug pull the developers raise money and drain the liquidity. In a honeypot the token is coded so you can buy but can't sell. A coin with no verifiable team that went from nowhere to everywhere in a day is a risk, not an opportunity.

Finally, be wary of any platform advertising fixed daily returns, including some "cloud mining" and "staking" schemes. At best they're unregulated. At worst they're Ponzi schemes where early payouts come from new deposits, and the collapse arrives when new money slows. Real investments don't promise a fixed daily profit.
Red flags to check in 60 seconds

items: Guaranteed or fixed returns, especially daily or weekly ones
Pressure to act now, or a countdown timer
A request to send crypto first so you can "unlock" or "verify" something
An anonymous team, no verifiable history, or a website that's only weeks old
Someone contacting you first with an opportunity, a support offer or a recovery service
A request for your seed phrase, private key or remote access to your device

content.text: One red flag is a reason to slow down. Two is usually a reason to walk away.
How to check a coin or platform in ten minutes

You can screen out most bad projects with a short routine. Search the project's name alongside words like "scam" or "withdrawal problems" and read recent results, not just the first page. Check that the website address matches the one linked from the project's official social accounts, and that those accounts have a real history rather than a recent burst of followers.

For a coin, look it up on a well-known data site and check how long it has existed, how much is traded daily and how the supply is split between the team and everyone else. For an exchange, check whether it's licensed in the places it operates and whether people have been able to withdraw large amounts. None of this is a guarantee, but projects that fail these checks are far more likely to cost you money than ones that pass them.
Setting up a safer routine

Most losses can be prevented by a few habits you set up once. Turn on two-factor authentication on every exchange, and use an authenticator app rather than SMS where you can, since phone numbers can be hijacked through SIM swaps. Use a separate email address for crypto accounts that you don't use anywhere else. Switch on withdrawal address whitelisting if your exchange offers it, so funds can only go to addresses you've pre-approved.

For anything you plan to hold for a long time, move it off the exchange into a wallet you control, ideally a hardware wallet, and keep the seed phrase offline. Keep only a small amount on exchanges for active trading. And before doing anything unfamiliar, send a small test amount first. Those few minutes cost almost nothing next to a mistake that can't be reversed.
What to do if you've already been scammed

Act quickly, but don't panic into a second mistake. Stop sending money, however convincing the reason for needing more. If you gave anyone your seed phrase or private key, move whatever remains to a brand-new wallet immediately and treat the old one as compromised. Change the passwords on any exchange or email account involved and check that two-factor authentication is still yours.

Then report it. Tell the exchange involved, since they can sometimes freeze funds that are still on the platform, and file a report with the police or financial-crime authority in your country. In Nigeria, that includes the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). Keep screenshots, wallet addresses and transaction IDs, because investigators need them. Be realistic: recovering money is hard, which is exactly why prevention matters, and why anyone offering to get it back for an upfront fee should be ignored.

faq.question: What are the most common cryptocurrency scams?
faq.answer: Phishing attacks, fake giveaways, pump and dump groups, fake wallets or exchanges, and recovery scams that target people who have already been defrauded.

faq.question: Why do beginners lose money in crypto?
faq.answer: Mostly through FOMO-driven buying without research, believing social media hype, using unverified platforms and failing to protect their seed phrases.

faq.question: How can I identify a crypto scam?
faq.answer: Scams tend to promise guaranteed returns, push you to act fast, hide who's behind the project, and ask you to send money before you receive anything. If you see any of these, treat it as a scam.

faq.question: Are all new crypto projects scams?
faq.answer: No, but new projects carry more risk because there's no track record. Look closely at the team, the whitepaper and the tokenomics before putting money into anything unproven.

faq.question: How can I protect my crypto investments?
faq.answer: Use a hardware wallet for larger amounts, turn on two-factor authentication on every exchange, never share your seed phrase, check the URL before you log in, and stick to well-known exchanges with a regulatory track record.

final_advice.text: In crypto, caution isn't paranoia. The people who hold on to their money here are rarely the ones chasing the fastest gain. They verify before they send, ignore anyone telling them to hurry, and never put in more than they could lose completely.
